items.label: section_header
items.text: CALCULATIONS FROM TITRATIONS

items.label: text
items.text: Titration is a technique that is used to find out how much of one solution reacts with a certain volume of another solution of known concentration. A solution of an alkali is measured into a conical flask using a pipette. An acid is run in from a burette, swirling the flask constantly. Towards the end, the acid is run in a drop at a time until the indicator just changes colour. If you know the concentration of either the acid or the alkali you can use the results of the titration to find the concentration of the solution you reacted it with.

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 6.9 The endpoint of a titration using methyl orange as indicator.

items.label: text
items.text: Acid-alkali titrations are discussed in Chapters 16 and 17.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE STANDARD CALCULATION

items.label: text
items.text: A standard titration problem will look like this:

items.label: text
items.text: 25.00 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution required 23.50 cm³ of dilutehydrochloric acid for neutralisation. Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid.

items.label: formula
items.text: N a O H ( a q ) + H C l ( a q ) \rightarrow N a C l ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( l )

items.label: text
items.text: We will use the same three-step method as we used above to calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid.

items.label: text
items.text: We know the volume (25.00 cm³) and concentration (0.100 mol/dm³) of the sodium hydroxide solution and so we can calculate the number of moles:

items.label: formula
items.text: \text {Sum of numer of $naO$ and $so$ with $naO$ and $so$} \colon & \quad ( 1 - \sum _ { \substack { \text {number of motes of NaOH} = \frac { 2 5 , 0 0 } { 1 0 0 0 } \times 0 . 1 0 0 = 0 . 0 0 2 5 0 \, m o l } } \\ & \quad ( 1 - \sum _ { \substack { \text {number of motes of NaOH} = \frac { 2 5 , 0 0 } { 1 0 0 0 } \times 0 . 1 0 0 = 0 . 0 0 2 5 0 \, m o l } }

items.label: text
items.text: From the chemical equation we know that 1 mol of NaOH reacts with 1 mol of HCl.

items.label: text
items.text: Therefore 0.00250 mol NaOH reacts with 0.00250 mol HCl.

items.label: text
items.text: Now that we have the number of moles of HCl we need to convert it to a concentration.

items.label: text
items.text: We know that we need 0.00250 mol of HCl to neutralise the NaOH. The volume of HCl we added was 23.50 cm³. So we know that this volume must contain 0.00250 mol of HCl.

items.label: text
items.text: We have the volume and number of moles of HCl and can work out the concentration:

items.label: formula
items.text: \text {concentration} \left ( m o l / d m ^ { 3 } \right ) = \frac { \text {number of holes} \left ( m o l \right ) } { \text {volume} \left ( d m ^ { 3 } \right ) }
